title: Surds

findings.finding: Multi-digit recurring notation is used without explaining which digits the bar makes repeat.
findings.breakdown: Students must distinguish 0.01̇4 from 0.overline(014), but the supplied demonstration establishes only a single recurring digit.
findings.checked: Searched all preceding teaching. p3-q2 supplies fraction-to-decimal practice, but its expected responses are not a permanent demonstration explaining the bar. Later classification answers do not provide earlier teaching.
findings.assumptions: The notation must be interpretable before students convert the given recurring decimals.

repair.proposal: Add to p3-information-block: “A bar marks the whole block that repeats: 0.overline(014) = 0.014014014… . In 0.01̇4 = 0.014444… , only the 4 repeats.” Render both expressions using the booklet's mathematical notation.

findings.doneWhen: Students can identify the repeating block before interpreting the multi-digit recurring stems.

findings.finding: The topic has no opening rehearsal of the decimal scaling and equation operations combined in its algebraic examples.
findings.breakdown: Following the examples requires multiplying recurring decimals by powers of ten, subtracting equations and dividing by a coefficient. The preceding pattern investigations do not rehearse these algebraic operations.
findings.checked: There are no opening review blocks. p3-q1-root through p4-q5-root investigate fraction–decimal patterns; the p5 examples combine the identified prerequisites.
findings.assumptions: Elementary equations are prior knowledge from the course's equation topics. The formal conversion method is explicitly taught without a calculator.

repair.proposal: Add four short opening items: (a) Calculate 10×0.046 and 100×0.046. [0.46; 4.6] (b) Simplify 100x−10x. [90x] (c) Given 10x=6.8 and x=0.68, subtract the second equation from the first. [9x=6.12] (d) Solve 90x=27. [x=3/10] Keep the complete review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review rehearses the substantial operations used together in the formal conversion examples.

findings.finding: Connect existing recurring decimals with the cancellation underlying the subtraction method.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up makes alignment of recurring tails explicit using numbers already converted.
findings.checked: 10×0.1overline(18)−0.overline(18)=1; 100×0.overline(18)−0.overline(18)=18. Both use the method taught on p5.
findings.assumptions: Exact recurring notation is used throughout.

repair.proposal: After p7-q9-y add: (z) Calculate 10×0.1overline(18)−0.overline(18). [1] (aa) Calculate 100×0.overline(18)−0.overline(18). [18] (ab) Explain why the recurring digits disappear in part aa. [Multiplication by 100 shifts the two-digit block by one complete repetition, so the identical recurring tails cancel.] Render overline notation mathematically.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up connects decimal shifting to exact cancellation.

findings.finding: Students must classify unfamiliar roots and rational multiples of roots without the exact-number facts needed to justify their decisions.
findings.breakdown: The instruction to use calculator decimals risks making a finite display the evidence for non-termination and non-recurrence.
findings.checked: The preceding definitions name √2 and π, and the number-set diagram includes √9. Neither establishes the non-perfect-square criterion or the effects of rational addition, multiplication and division. Hidden worked answers are not supplied teaching.
findings.assumptions: Classification is new in this topic; calculator use is explicit.

repair.proposal: Before p9-identify-root add: “A calculator displays only finitely many digits; its display alone cannot establish that a decimal never terminates or repeats. The square root of a positive whole number is rational if the number is a perfect square, and irrational otherwise: √9=3, whereas √3 is irrational. Adding a rational number to an irrational number, or multiplying or dividing an irrational number by a nonzero rational number, leaves it irrational. Thus √5+1, √2/2 and 2√2 are irrational.”

findings.doneWhen: Students can justify the classifications from exact-number facts rather than the appearance of a calculator display.

findings.finding: Compare positive surd expressions through their equal squares.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the inverse relationship with equivalent exact expressions.
findings.checked: (2√18)²=72 and (6√2)²=72. Both expressions are positive, so equality follows from the positive square-root relationship already taught.
findings.assumptions: No extraction method from the next topic is required.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts: (f) Evaluate (2√18)². [72] (g) Evaluate (6√2)². [72] (h) Both expressions are positive. Are they equal? Explain why. [Yes; both are the positive square root of 72.]

findings.doneWhen: Students connect equal squares and positivity to equality of these two expressions.

findings.finding: Higher-root simplification is required after teaching only square-factor extraction.
findings.breakdown: Students need to match the extracted factor's power to the root's index. Applying the stated highest-square-factor procedure to a cube root would give an invalid extraction.
findings.checked: p14 recognises cube roots, p17 names the index and p18 states square-root laws. p21 teaches square-root extraction only; p25-q14-a evaluates perfect cubes without modelling partial extraction.
findings.assumptions: Evaluating familiar roots is prior knowledge; extracting factors from non-perfect higher roots is a new variant. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p25-q14 add: “Match the factor's power to the root's index: use perfect cubes for cube roots and perfect fifth powers for fifth roots.” Model ∛54=∛(27×2)=3∛2 and ⁵√96=⁵√(32×3)=2⁵√3. Include the symbolic application ∛(a⁶b³)=a²b for positive a and b.

findings.doneWhen: Students see index-matched extraction, including a fifth root and the symbolic form, before the targeted questions.

findings.finding: Parts d and e both ask students to simplify √72 without an explicit instructional purpose for the repeated task.
findings.breakdown: The complete expressions and required operations are unchanged.
findings.checked: Both prompts are √72 under the same instruction. No retrieval or comparison purpose is stated.
findings.assumptions: Part labels determine the later copy: p24-q8-f is labelled e.

repair.proposal: Change p24-q8-f, the part labelled e, to √50. Answer: 5√2.

findings.doneWhen: The later copy retains square-root simplification with a different radicand.

findings.finding: Three supplied completion lines omit radical signs around factors that must remain under roots.
findings.breakdown: Completing the blanks as specified produces false intermediate equalities and suggests that nonsquare factors can be moved outside a radical unchanged.
findings.checked: For √8×√18 the valid intermediate product is 2√2×3√2, giving 12. For √8×√24 it is √8×√3√8, giving 8√3. For √12×√18 it is √2√6×√3√6, giving 6√6. The preceding correct examples do not make the false scaffolds valid.
findings.assumptions: The supplied prompts accurately represent the visible completion lines; no source-fidelity claim is made.

repair.proposal: Change p32-q3-c to “=2√[[2]]×3√[[2]]”; p34-q6-a-response to “=√8×√[[3]]√8”; and p34-q6-b-response to “=√[[2]]√6×√[[3]]√6”. Retain the existing final-answer blanks.

findings.doneWhen: Every completed intermediate line preserves the original product and demonstrates the intended method.

findings.finding: Two exercise parts repeat complete guided tasks with unchanged expressions.
findings.breakdown: The later copies offer no fresh multiplication instance.
findings.checked: Compared the complete tasks √7×√3 and √12×√8, including their shared simplification instructions. No explicit retrieval or comparison purpose is supplied.
findings.assumptions: Guided practice precedes the exercise.

repair.proposal: Replace p32-q1-b with √7×√5 [√35], and p32-q2-f with √12×√10 [2√30]. Retain the guided tasks.

findings.doneWhen: Both later parts require fresh calculations with the same structures.

findings.finding: Two independent exercise parts repeat complete earlier surd-division tasks without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: p37-q1-a repeats √20÷√2, and p37-q1-b repeats √15÷√3.
findings.checked: Compared the complete expressions and instructions in all four copies. No explicit retrieval or comparison purpose is supplied.
findings.assumptions: Guided and earlier-topic student tasks are included in the duplicate criterion.

repair.proposal: Change p37-q1-a to √22÷√2, answer √11. Change p37-q1-b to √21÷√3, answer √7. Retain the earlier copies.

findings.doneWhen: Both later copies practise direct surd division with different values.

findings.finding: The distributive-law examples combine earlier surd multiplication and square-factor extraction without rehearsing both methods.
findings.breakdown: Students must recall coefficient multiplication, multiplication of radicands and extraction while learning to distribute across a bracket.
findings.checked: The examples directly use these methods in 3√15+√18 and 6√60−12√36. Earlier topics teach them, but this topic has no review. The combined-method exception applies even though division practice immediately before it also involves simplification.
findings.assumptions: Exact symbolic work is intended; calculators do not perform the required decisions.

repair.proposal: Before p41-expanding add: “Simplify: (a) √18; (b) √3×√5; (c) 2√6×3√10.” Answers: 3√2; √15; 12√15. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Both earlier methods are rehearsed before their combined use in the examples.

findings.finding: Two independent expansion parts repeat complete guided-practice tasks without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both expressions, including their values and signs, are unchanged between guided and independent practice.
findings.checked: Compared each guided expression with its exercise copy. No retrieval or comparison purpose is stated.
findings.assumptions: Guided practice precedes the exercise.

repair.proposal: Change p42-q1-a to √3(√15−√3), answer 3√5−3. Change p42-q1-d to √10(√8−2), answer 4√5−2√10. Retain the guided originals.

findings.doneWhen: Each later copy has different numbers while preserving its expansion structure.

findings.finding: The first independent binomial expansion repeats the complete guided task without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both copies ask for the expansion of (√3+1)(√2−1).
findings.checked: Compared the complete expressions and their enclosing instructions. No retrieval or comparison purpose is stated.
findings.assumptions: Guided practice precedes independent practice.
findings.doneWhen: The independent part retains the same expansion structure with different values.

findings.finding: Test the related numerical value and compare the product of the two values.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up exposes cancellation of opposite surd terms through substitution and expansion.
findings.checked: For x=−3−2√2, x²=17+12√2 and 6x=−18−12√2, so x²+6x+1=0. The proposed product is 9−8=1. Ordinary expansion suffices; later conjugate terminology is unnecessary.
findings.assumptions: The original question becomes part a.
findings.doneWhen: The optional parts compare the two concrete values using methods already taught.

findings.finding: Two rationalisation tasks repeat complete earlier questions without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: 5/√5 appears in both p49-q5-b and p50-q6-k; (1+√2)/√3 appears in both p48-guided-part-c and p51-q9-a.
findings.checked: Compared all four complete tasks. The earlier matching-numerator exercise has an explicit application purpose, but no purpose is stated for repeating its unchanged task later. The guided-to-independent copy likewise has no stated repetition purpose.
findings.assumptions: Exact repetition across guided and independent practice is included in the duplicate criterion.

repair.proposal: Change p50-q6-k to 7/√7, answer √7. Change p51-q9-a to (1+√3)/√2, answer (√2+√6)/2. Retain both earlier copies.

findings.doneWhen: Both later copies retain their original structures with different numbers.

findings.finding: The final symbolic expression combines squared surd fractions, reciprocal cross-products and cancellation against an outside variable product without an intermediate combined task.
findings.breakdown: Earlier numerical expansions and single symbolic rationalisations do not bridge the simultaneous changes in representation and coordination required here.
findings.checked: Read the supplied rationalising practice. p49-q5 introduces symbolic cancellation, but no preceding task combines a squared difference of fractional surds with an outside cancelling factor. This is a sharp combined demand even though its component methods were taught. For x,y>0 the expression equals x²−2xy+y².
findings.assumptions: Ordinary algebraic fractions and square expansion are prior learning. The original real-valued expression requires x,y>0.

repair.proposal: Before p51-q13-root add: “Simplify: (a) 6(√3/√2−√2/√3)². [1] (b) 2x(√x/√2−√2/√x)², for x>0. [(x−2)²].” Part a combines the operations numerically; part b replaces one numerical parameter with a variable before the existing two-variable task.

findings.doneWhen: A numerical combined task and a one-variable version precede the two-variable expression.

findings.finding: The infinite nested radical requires a repeating-tail interpretation that preceding instruction does not supply.
findings.breakdown: Squaring finite nested radicals does not show how the infinite expression supplies x=√(1+x). This is a new representation-to-equation decision, rather than merely a harder calculation using the demonstrated method.
findings.checked: p57-q11-root and p58-q12-root concern finite radicals. Earlier recurring-decimal examples cancel recurring tails but do not identify an infinite nested radical with its own tail.
findings.assumptions: Quadratic solving is available from the course's separate equation topics. The stated radical is interpreted as its positive limiting value.

repair.proposal: Append: “The expression under the first square root is 1 plus the same repeating radical. Write x=√(1+x), then square both sides and solve, remembering that x is positive.” The resulting answer is (1+√5)/2.

findings.doneWhen: The repeating-tail interpretation is supplied, leaving students to form and solve the quadratic.

findings.finding: Compare the sum and difference of reciprocal expressions using the existing numerical value of x.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects rationalisation with cancellation and the middle term in squared binomials.
findings.checked: For x=√7+√6, 1/x=√7−√6. Hence x−1/x=2√6, its square is 24, and the previously established squared sum is 28. All expressions are defined because x is positive.
findings.assumptions: Use the value of x already supplied in Question 10.

repair.proposal: After p57-q10-b-ii append (iii) “Find x−1/x.” [2√6] (iv) “Find (x−1/x)².” [24] (v) “How much larger is (x+1/x)² than (x−1/x)²?” [4]

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up compares the two squared expressions using the existing value of x.

findings.finding: Multi-digit recurring notation is required before the repeating bar is explained.
findings.breakdown: Students meet single-digit recurrence first, then must interpret repeating blocks, including leading zeros. No preceding instruction explains which digits the bar makes repeat.
findings.checked: p3-information-block and p3-q1-root introduce single-digit recurrence. The calculator investigations show decimal patterns but do not explain bar notation.
findings.assumptions: Recurring notation is being introduced in this sequence; answer annotations are not supplied teaching.

repair.proposal: Before p3-q2-h add: “A bar shows the whole block that repeats: 0.\overline{142857}=0.142857142857… . Include zeros within the repeating block: 0.\overline{01}=0.010101… .”

findings.doneWhen: The repeating bar and leading zeros are explicitly interpreted before students use them.

findings.finding: Question 6 requires conversion of decimals with non-recurring prefixes before that conversion method is supplied.
findings.breakdown: The preceding investigations establish fractions for pure recurring blocks. They do not show how to account for a non-recurring prefix such as the tenth in 0.1\dot{4}.
findings.checked: p4-q3-root through p4-q5-root investigate pure repeats. p5-example-right and p7-q8-root subsequently supply the relevant algebraic preparation.
findings.assumptions: The stated booklet order is the teaching order.

repair.proposal: Move the complete p5-q6-block immediately after p7-q8-block. Preserve its internal comparisons and use it as mixed consolidation.

findings.doneWhen: All prefix conversions in Question 6 follow the relevant worked example and Question 8.

findings.finding: The algebraic examples supply their powers of ten without stating how those multipliers are chosen.
findings.breakdown: Students see successful subtraction but must independently choose multipliers for longer prefixes and repeating blocks. The origin of those multiplier choices is not stated.
findings.checked: The two p5 examples display matching recurring tails. p6-g supplies 100x and p7-q8 supplies 10x and 100x, but neither explains the selection decision.
findings.assumptions: Students must choose their own multipliers in later unscaffolded parts.

repair.proposal: At p5-example-group add: “Choose two multiples of x with identical recurring digits after the decimal point. First shift any non-recurring decimal digits before the point; then shift one complete repeating block further. Subtraction cancels the matching tails.” Annotate the left example “Use x and 10x: one repeating digit”; the right “Use 10x and 100x: one non-recurring digit, then one repeating digit”; and p6-g “Use x and 100x: two repeating digits.”

findings.doneWhen: The multiplier choices are explicitly connected to prefix length and repeating-block length.

findings.finding: Connect the recurring-nine result with its terminating representation.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up exposes that two different decimal representations can denote exactly the same number.
findings.checked: The existing part gives 0.0\dot{9}=1/10. Since 0.1=1/10, their difference is exactly zero. Only fraction conversion and subtraction are needed.
findings.assumptions: Use the existing part's fraction result.

repair.proposal: After the existing part labelled d, append (e) “Write 0.1 as a fraction.” [1/10] (f) “Find 0.1−0.0\dot{9}. Explain why using your fractions.” [0, because both numbers equal 1/10.]

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up compares the two representations using exact fractions.

findings.finding: The identification task requires facts about irrational roots and their transformations that preceding teaching does not supply.
findings.breakdown: Definitions and the named example √2 do not establish that √5, √5+1, √2/2 and 2√2 are irrational. A finite calculator display cannot establish the required infinite decimal behaviour.
findings.checked: p3-q1-c already addresses the finite calculator display, and the fraction definition supplies a route for p9-identify-o, so those portions of the original claim are removed. p8 supplies no general classification rule for the targeted root expressions.
findings.assumptions: Calculator approximations support exploration but do not establish irrationality.

repair.proposal: Before p9-identify-root add: “Use the calculator to approximate; its display alone cannot establish irrationality. A square root of a positive integer that is not a perfect square is irrational. Adding an integer, or multiplying or dividing by a non-zero integer, preserves irrationality. Thus √5, √5+1, 2√2 and √2/2 are irrational.”

findings.doneWhen: Students have an explicit classification basis for the unfamiliar root expressions before deciding their rationality.

findings.finding: Reverse simplification and collection by choosing a radicand that produces a target coefficient.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the square factor inside a radical with the coefficient of a like surd.
findings.checked: The fixed terms total 10√6. Targets 20√6 and 30√6 require √N=2√6 and √N=4√6 respectively, giving N=24 and N=96. Both are positive whole numbers.
findings.assumptions: Students may reason backwards using the simplification and collection methods taught in this topic.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts after p28-q7-l: (m) “Replace 36 in 6√6+2√24+5√36 with a positive whole number so that the expression simplifies to 20√6.” [24] (n) “Replace 36 in the same expression so that it simplifies to 30√6.” [96]

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts require students to choose and verify the two radicands.

findings.finding: Three supplied completion lines omit radical signs, turning radical factors into ordinary coefficients.
findings.breakdown: Completing the printed blanks produces false equalities: the p32 line gives 24 instead of 12; the p34 lines replace √24 by 3√8 and replace √12 and √18 by 2√6 and 3√6.
findings.checked: Direct calculation confirms all three errors. p21, p31 and p34-example-demonstration model valid radical factorisation, but cannot make these printed equalities valid.
findings.assumptions: The supplied prompts accurately represent the student-facing completion lines.

repair.proposal: In p32-q3-c print '=2√[[2]]×3√[[2]]', giving 12. In p34-q6-a-response print '=√8×√[[3]]√8', giving 8√3. In p34-q6-b-response print '=√[[2]]√6×√[[3]]√6', giving 6√6. Retain the final-answer blanks.

findings.doneWhen: Filling the existing numerical blanks produces valid equalities, with all required radical signs supplied.

findings.finding: Vary the outside coefficient while holding the bracket fixed to expose scaling and sign changes.
findings.breakdown: The existing practice includes negative multipliers but no consecutive comparison that isolates their effect on both terms.
findings.checked: All five proposed expansions are correct and use taught distribution, multiplication and simplification. The added instruction is one prediction line.
findings.assumptions: Append these parts under Question 1's existing expansion instruction.

repair.proposal: After part j add: “Predict how each result will change before expanding.” Append (k) √3(√6−√3) [3√2−3]; (l) 2√3(√6−√3) [6√2−6]; (m) −√3(√6−√3) [−3√2+3]; (n) −2√3(√6−√3) [−6√2+6]. Follow with unpatterned (o) −3√5(2√10+√5) [−30√2−15]. In k–n only the outside coefficient varies; the bracket and outside radicand stay fixed.

findings.doneWhen: The four-part comparison is followed by the unpatterned transfer question.

findings.finding: The topic lacks an opening rehearsal of the earlier operations combined in its rationalisation examples.
findings.breakdown: The examples combine value-preserving fraction multiplication, distribution and surd multiplication while introducing conjugate selection. The conjugate-product questions rehearse the denominator calculation but not these other steps.
findings.checked: p48 teaches monomial rationalisation and p41 and p31 teach the other operations. Although monomial rationalisation immediately precedes this topic, the combined-method exception requires rehearsal of the earlier methods used together.
findings.assumptions: These operations are prior knowledge; exact arithmetic is used. Calculator access does not supply the algebraic decisions.

repair.proposal: Before p52-conjugate-definition add: (a) Simplify √5×2√2. [2√10] (b) Expand 3(4−√7). [12−3√7] (c) Rationalise 2/√3. [2√3/3] Include the short completion “Multiplying by √3/√3 preserves value because this multiplier equals ___.” [1] Keep the complete review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review rehearses the three earlier operations before their combined use.

protectedGroups.observation: A rational root remains rational when multiplied by an integer or added to an integer.
protectedGroups.varies: The operation outside sqrt(16).
protectedGroups.invariant: The radicand 16 and its rational square root.

protectedGroups.observation: A cube-root symbol does not by itself make a number a surd.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether the radicand is a perfect cube.
protectedGroups.invariant: Cube-root notation and the classification task.

protectedGroups.observation: Zero is unchanged by a minus sign, while a negative radicand and a negative sign outside a square root have different effects on real-valuedness.
protectedGroups.varies: Zero versus one and the position of the minus sign.

protectedGroups.observation: A fractional radicand can have either a rational or an irrational square root.
protectedGroups.varies: The numerator, from a perfect square to a non-square.
protectedGroups.invariant: The denominator 16 or 25 is a perfect square and the task is classification.

protectedGroups.observation: A terminating decimal and a recurring decimal can both be rational while representing different numbers.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether the digit 3 terminates or repeats.
protectedGroups.invariant: The visible digit and rational classification.

protectedGroups.observation: A square-root sign alone does not determine rationality.
protectedGroups.varies: Non-perfect-square versus perfect-square radicand.

protectedGroups.observation: Equivalent decimal and percentage representations retain the same value and classification.
protectedGroups.varies: Decimal versus percentage notation.

protectedGroups.observation: Different root expressions can have the same decimal approximation and number-line position.
protectedGroups.varies: 2sqrt(6) versus sqrt(24).
protectedGroups.invariant: Exact value, rationality, rounded values and location.

protectedGroups.observation: The position of 3 determines whether it is the root index or an external coefficient.
protectedGroups.varies: The position of 3 and the corresponding root index.

protectedGroups.observation: The radicand is the complete expression beneath the radical.
protectedGroups.varies: The algebraic expression beneath the radical.

protectedGroups.observation: Squaring a square root and taking the square root of a square both recover the given positive number.
protectedGroups.varies: The order of rooting and squaring within each pair, then the number.
protectedGroups.invariant: The positive number within each pair and the inverse relationship.

protectedGroups.observation: Reversing division reverses the quotient beneath the radical.
protectedGroups.varies: The order of the two roots.
protectedGroups.invariant: The radicands 21 and 3 and the division operation.

protectedGroups.observation: A coefficient inside the squared brackets is squared along with the root.
protectedGroups.varies: The coefficient inside the square: 1, 2 and 3.
protectedGroups.invariant: The radicand 10 and the square applied to the whole bracket.

protectedGroups.observation: Moving the coefficient outside the squared expression changes whether that coefficient is squared.
protectedGroups.varies: The scope of the exponent.

protectedGroups.observation: A coefficient outside the squared root multiplies the recovered radicand unchanged.
protectedGroups.varies: The external coefficient.

protectedGroups.observation: The numerator determines the single recurring digit for ninths.
protectedGroups.varies: Numerator.

protectedGroups.observation: Fractions over 99 produce a two-digit repeating block, retaining a leading zero when necessary.
protectedGroups.varies: Numerator.

protectedGroups.observation: Fractions over 999 produce three-digit repeating blocks, including leading zeros.
protectedGroups.varies: Number of digits in the numerator.

protectedGroups.observation: Moving the start of repetition and changing a preceding digit change the fraction even when the repeating digit stays the same.
protectedGroups.varies: Position of repetition and non-repeating prefix.

protectedGroups.observation: The same initial decimal digits represent different numbers when different digits repeat.
protectedGroups.varies: Scope of the recurrence mark.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the whole-number part differs from delaying the recurring contribution.
protectedGroups.varies: Whole-number part, then position of repetition.

protectedGroups.observation: Five repeated comparison groups distinguish immediate repetition, delayed repetition, a nonzero prefix and a two-digit repeating block.
protectedGroups.varies: Prefix and repeating-block length within each group; digits between groups.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the outside coefficient scales the simplified result without changing the remaining radical.
protectedGroups.varies: The outside coefficient is 1, 2, then 3.

protectedGroups.observation: The outside coefficient contributes the same square factor when roots are combined.
protectedGroups.varies: The radicand changes from 3 to 5.
protectedGroups.invariant: The coefficient is 3 and contributes a factor of 9 inside the combined root.

protectedGroups.observation: Coefficient collection works in the same way for algebraic terms and like surds, including an unwritten coefficient of 1.
protectedGroups.varies: The subtracted coefficient and whether coefficient 1 is written.
protectedGroups.invariant: The paired algebraic and surd structures.

protectedGroups.observation: Simplifying first determines which coefficients can be collected; swapping coefficients between differently scaled roots can change the result.
protectedGroups.varies: Radicands, coefficients and which roots require simplification, through linked comparisons.
protectedGroups.invariant: A sum of two positive root terms requiring the same simplify-then-collect procedure.

protectedGroups.observation: Perfect-square roots become rational terms, which must be collected separately from remaining surds.
protectedGroups.varies: An added perfect-square term, followed by replacing another radicand with a perfect square.
protectedGroups.invariant: The term 2sqrt(24), and then the added term 5sqrt(36).

protectedGroups.observation: Changing one radicand at a time changes whether the result is rational and which square factor can be extracted.
protectedGroups.varies: One radicand between consecutive parts.
protectedGroups.invariant: A product of two square roots.

protectedGroups.observation: A fixed first factor produces both rational and irrational products as the second factor changes.
protectedGroups.varies: The second radicand: 4, 5, 10, 20, 40.

protectedGroups.observation: The radicand comparison is retained while students separately multiply fixed coefficients.
protectedGroups.varies: The second radicand: 5, 10, 20.

protectedGroups.observation: Simplifying before division and dividing before simplification give the same result.
protectedGroups.varies: Order of the two operations.
protectedGroups.invariant: The expression sqrt(12)/sqrt(3) and its value.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the exponent from odd to even can remove the remaining square root.
protectedGroups.varies: Exponent 3 becomes 4.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing term order preserves a product, whereas changing a sign changes the signed products.
protectedGroups.varies: Term order first, then one sign.
protectedGroups.invariant: The numbers 1, 2 and √5 and the two-binomial structure.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the shared radicand changes the rational product while preserving the cross-term coefficient.
protectedGroups.varies: The shared radicand changes from 5 to 7.
protectedGroups.invariant: The constants, signs and unit surd coefficients.
